hints: Think about the general pattern when a reactive metal such as calcium reacts with a dilute acid to form a salt.
walkthrough:
Spot the familiar reaction type**
You have calcium metal reacting with dilute nitric acid, $\text{HNO}_3$, to give the salt calcium nitrate. This is just a classic metal plus acid reaction, so sit it alongside magnesium with $\text{HCl}$ or zinc with $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ in your mind.

Pair up the ions left over**
Calcium displaces hydrogen from the acid to form $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ and $\text{NO}_3^-$. The $\text{H}^+$ ions left behind gain electrons to form the other product, hydrogen gas, $\text{H}_2$.
Final answer: hydrogen, $\text{H}_2$

hints: Recall the three standard products formed when any Group 2 nitrate is heated strongly.
walkthrough:
Remember what nitrates break into**
Heating a Group 2 nitrate never gives the metal back. It always splits into the metal oxide plus nitrogen dioxide and oxygen. So for calcium you expect $\text{CaO}$, $\text{NO}_2$ and $\text{O}_2$.

Balance the atoms**
Start with one $\text{Ca(NO}_3\text{)}_2$. That gives one $\text{CaO}$, which leaves $2\text{N}$ and $5\text{O}$ to account for. That needs $2\text{NO}_2$ plus $\frac{1}{2}\text{O}_2$: $$\text{Ca(NO}_3\text{)}_2 \rightarrow \text{CaO} + 2\text{NO}_2 + \frac{1}{2}\text{O}_2$$

hints: Think about how cation size and polarising power change from magnesium to barium and how this affects distortion of the nitrate ion.
walkthrough:
Link stability to the cation**
Down Group 2 the cations get larger, for example $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ is small and $\text{Ba}^{2+}$ is large. A smaller cation has higher charge density and polarises and distorts the $\text{NO}_3^-$ ion more, making it easier to break apart on heating.

State the trend**
Because polarising power decreases down the group, the nitrates become harder to decompose. So thermal stability increases down the group and a higher temperature is needed.
Final answer: Thermal stability increases down Group 2.

hints: Look at the scheme: solid $\text{CaCO}_3$ plus water plus excess $\text{CO}_2$ all combine to give aqueous $\text{Ca(HCO}_3\text{)}_2$.
walkthrough:
Collect all the reactants**
Reaction 3 shows $\text{CaCO}_3\text{(s)}$ reacting with excess $\text{CO}_2\text{(g)}$ in the presence of $\text{H}_2\text{O(l)}$ to form soluble $\text{Ca(HCO}_3\text{)}_2\text{(aq)}$. Nothing else is involved.

Write the combined equation**
Simply add the three reactants together on the left: $$\text{CaCO}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{CO}_2 \rightarrow \text{Ca(HCO}_3\text{)}_2$$ Check atoms: $1\text{Ca}$, $2\text{C}$, $2\text{H}$ and $6\text{O}$ on each side, so it is already balanced.

hints: Recall whether $\text{Ca(OH)}_2$ is acidic or basic and what problem acidic soil causes for crops.
walkthrough:
See $\text{Ca(OH)}_2$ as a base**
Calcium hydroxide, slaked lime, is an alkali that provides $\text{OH}^-$ ions. It will neutralise excess $\text{H}^+$ ions in the soil.

Link to farming**
Many soils become too acidic for healthy plant growth. Farmers spread $\text{Ca(OH)}_2$ to reduce acidity, raise pH toward neutral and improve growing conditions.
Final answer: Used to neutralise / reduce acidity of acidic soil.

hints: Break the symbol sp into its parts and think about which atomic orbitals must merge to make that hybrid.
walkthrough:
Unpack the name**
The label sp tells you exactly what is mixed. One s atomic orbital and one p atomic orbital on the same carbon atom merge together.

Form the hybrids**
Their wave functions combine to give two equivalent sp hybrid orbitals, leaving two unhybridised p orbitals for pi bonding in the $\text{C}_2^{2-}$ ion.
Final answer: Mixing / overlap / combination of one s and one p orbital.

hints: Recall the difference between head-on (end-on) overlap that gives a sigma bond and sideways overlap that gives a pi bond.
Picture two dumbbell shaped sp orbitals pointing toward each other along the same axis and overlapping in the region between the nuclei.
walkthrough:
Aim the orbitals at each other**
Take one sp hybrid orbital on each carbon and point them directly at each other along the line joining the two nuclei. This is head-on or end-on approach, not sideways.

Show the sigma overlap**
Draw the two lobes meeting and overlapping in the middle. Shade or outline the overlap region to show the sigma bond, where electron density is concentrated directly between the nuclei on the axis.
Final answer: Two sp hybrid orbitals overlap head-on / end-on along the internuclear axis to form a sigma bond, with increased electron density between the two nuclei.

hints: Start from the mass of $\text{NH}_3$ in grams using $1 \text{ tonne} = 1.00 \times 10^6 \text{ g}$ and divide by $M_r = 17.0$ to get moles of $\text{NH}_3$.
Use the equation $\text{CaCN}_2 + 3\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{CaCO}_3 + 2\text{NH}_3$ to find the mole ratio of $\text{CaCN}_2$ to $\text{NH}_3$, then convert back to tonnes.
walkthrough:
Convert product mass to moles**
First change tonnes to grams: $$1.50 \times 10^6 \text{ tonnes} = 1.50 \times 10^6 \times 10^6 \text{ g} = 1.50 \times 10^{12} \text{ g}$$ Then divide by $M_r(\text{NH}_3)=17.0$: $$n(\text{NH}_3) = \frac{1.50 \times 10^{12}}{17.0} = 8.82 \times 10^{10} \text{ mol}$$

Scale to $\text{CaCN}_2$ and back to tonnes**
From the equation, $1$ mol $\text{CaCN}_2$ gives $2$ mol $\text{NH}_3$, so: $$n(\text{CaCN}_2) = \frac{1}{2} \times 8.82 \times 10^{10} = 4.41 \times 10^{10} \text{ mol}$$ With $M_r(\text{CaCN}_2)=80.1$: $$m = 4.41 \times 10^{10} \times 80.1 = 3.53 \times 10^{12} \text{ g} = 3.53 \times 10^6 \text{ tonnes}$$
Final answer: moles $\text{NH}_3 = 8.82 \times 10^{10}$; minimum mass of $\text{CaCN}_2 = 3.53 \times 10^6$ tonnes

hints: For $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{Br}$ with $\text{CN}^-$ in ethanol, think about which atom replaces Br and how the carbon chain length changes.
For heating a nitrile with aqueous $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ under reflux, recall the fully hydrolysed functional group containing C=O and OH.
For propanone with NaCN and HCN, recall the addition product across C=O that contains both OH and CN on the same carbon.
walkthrough:
Extend the chain with cyanide**
$\text{CN}^-$ from $\text{NaCN}$ acts as a nucleophile and displaces $\text{Br}^-$ from bromoethane. The $\text{CN}$ group adds one carbon, giving propanenitrile: $$\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{Br} \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CN}$$

Hydrolyse the nitrile to the acid**
Heating $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CN}$ with $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4\text{(aq)}$ under reflux fully hydrolyses $\text{-CN}$ to $\text{-CO}_2\text{H}$, giving propanoic acid: $$\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CN} \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CO}_2\text{H}$$

Add HCN to the ketone**
Propanone, $\text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_3$, undergoes nucleophilic addition of HCN catalysed by $\text{CN}^-$. Both $\text{OH}$ and $\text{CN}$ end up on the original carbonyl carbon, giving the cyanohydrin: $$\text{(CH}_3\text{)}_2\text{C=O} \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{C(OH)(CN)CH}_3$$

Final answer: From $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{Br}$: $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CN}$; then $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CO}_2\text{H}$; from $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{C=O}$: $\text{CH}_3\text{C(OH)(CN)CH}_3$
